main_ilo: Explain that organs are built from several tissue types, and that tissue is made of cells, ECM and signalling molecules

concepts.statement: Organs are built from several different tissue types working together
There are four tissue categories: epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous
Tissue is made of cells, extracellular matrix (ECM) and signalling molecules

scenes.text: Paris, c. 1800. Surgeons can name every organ, but they cannot explain why the lining of the gut and the lining of the airway fall ill in the same way. Xavier Bichat has a table covered in specimens and a hunch: perhaps the organ is not the smallest useful unit of the body.

dialogue.speaker: Xavier Bichat
dialogue.line: If two different organs fail the same way, what might they share?

scenes.text: Bichat first treats each organ as one substance. It doesn't work: a stomach wall behaves like several materials at once. He dries, boils and soaks samples in acid, and notices that layers from different organs react alike.

dialogue.speaker: Xavier Bichat
dialogue.line: The stomach does not answer as one thing. Why would its layers disagree?

scenes.text: Bichat sorts the layers by how they behave, not by which organ they came from, and calls each group a tissue: one organ, many tissues. Decades later, in 1839, Theodor Schwann adds the next piece: animal tissues are made of cells.

dialogue.speaker: Xavier Bichat
dialogue.line: Sort them by what they do, not where they were found.

dialogue.speaker: Theodor Schwann
dialogue.line: And look closer still. Those layers are built from cells.

scenes.text: Your course states it precisely: organs are assemblies of four tissue categories, and every tissue combines cells with an extracellular matrix and the signalling molecules that coordinate them. Designing a biomaterial means designing for that whole system, not just the cells.

clues.title: Bichat's acid-test notes
clues.text: Layers from the gut and the airway blister the same way in acid, although they come from different organs.

clues.title: Relabelled specimen jars
clues.text: Jars sorted by layer type instead of organ: linings together, supporting layers together, contracting layers together.

clues.title: Schwann's cell sketch
clues.text: A drawing of animal tissue: many small units, each with a nucleus, packed among fibres.

clues.title: Introduction lecture
clues.text: Tissue = cells + ECM + signalling molecules. Four tissue categories: epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous.

mentor_question.question: If a lung and a gut fall ill in the same way, what does that tell you about how organs are built?
key_points: Organs are made of more than one tissue type
The same tissue type can appear in different organs
The shared tissue, not the organ, explains the shared behaviour
hints: Think about the layers, not the whole organ.
Which layers reacted the same way in the acid test?

options: Organs share tissue types, so the same tissue can fail in different organs
Each organ is made of one unique substance
Disease only affects whole organs, never their layers
Organs with the same shape always behave the same

field_notes.note: An organ is not one material: it is several tissue types working together, and the same tissue can appear in many organs.
Four tissue categories: epithelial (linings), connective (support, e.g. bone and cartilage), muscle (contraction) and nervous (signalling).
Every tissue is cells plus extracellular matrix (ECM) plus signalling molecules. Change one and the tissue behaves differently.

what_really_happened.summary: Bichat (c. 1800) classified the body into tissues by dissecting and chemically testing organs, without relying on a microscope. In 1839 Schwann proposed that animals are made of cells, which later explained what tissues are built from. The dialogue in this era is dramatised.

briefing.title: The scaffold that wouldn't take
briefing.situation: A start-up seeds a patient's own cells onto a plastic scaffold to repair knee cartilage. In trials the cells survive, but the implant never behaves like cartilage.
briefing.task: Work out why with Alex, and recommend what the next design must include.
briefing.objective: Explain the failure using what tissue is made of.

evidence.title: Week 6 lab report
evidence.text: Seeded cells are alive, but almost no new matrix (collagen, proteoglycan) has formed around them.

evidence.title: Healthy cartilage histology
evidence.text: Healthy cartilage is a connective tissue: mostly matrix with few cells, which respond to growth factors held in that matrix.

evidence.title: Marketing brochure
evidence.text: The scaffold comes in five colours and ships worldwide.

evidence.title: Joint anatomy note
evidence.text: A knee joint combines cartilage, bone, ligament and synovial lining, each a different tissue.

stage2_alex_decides.decision_prompt: Alex must choose what to change in the next scaffold design.
stage2_alex_decides.correct_decision: Add matrix components and signalling molecules (growth factors) so the cells can build and maintain cartilage tissue, not just survive.

likely_mistakes.alex_says: The cells are alive, so the tissue is fine. Let's just add more cells.
likely_mistakes.why_wrong: Tissue is not just cells. Without ECM and signals the cells will not form cartilage.

likely_mistakes.alex_says: Make the scaffold from bone material. Bone is strong, so it will last.
likely_mistakes.why_wrong: Cartilage and bone are different connective tissues with different matrices.

likely_mistakes.alex_says: Treat the whole knee as one material and match its average stiffness.
likely_mistakes.why_wrong: The knee is several tissues. The implant must match the specific tissue it replaces.

stage3_curveball.new_condition: The surgeon now wants the implant to bond to the bone underneath as well as replace the cartilage.
stage3_curveball.correct_response: Recognise two different tissues: design a layered implant with a cartilage-like layer and a bone-like layer, each with the right matrix.
